To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cost of a superconducting magnet is proportional to the magnet stored energy, that the cost of the helium refrigeration needed to keep the superconducting magnet cold is proportional to the refrigeration needed at 4.4K, and that the annual cost of the 4.5 K refrigeration is proportional to the 4.4 K refrigeration needed and the electrical energy cost.

the cost of a superconducting magnet can be estimated by multiplying the stored energy by a constant, and the cost of a 4.5 K refrigeration system can be estimated by dividing the annual 4.5-K refrigeration by a constant.

for a given stored energy, the cost of a superconducting magnet is approximately $0.5 per watt, the cost of the cold box and compressor needed to keep the superconducting magnet cold is $0.2 per watt, and the annual operating cost of a 4.5 K refrigeration system is $0.01 per watt.

estimating the cost of superconductors, superconducting magnets, and refrigeration.
determining the cost of superconductors and refrigerators needed to cool them.
the development of a computer program to predict the cost of superconductors and the refrigeration needed to keep them cool.

the cost of a superconducting magnet is proportional to its stored energy and the cost of the refrigeration needed to cool the magnet is proportional to the 4.5 K refrigeration generated by the magnet.

the cost of superconductors has not changed much over the last 20 years.
the cost of the magnet and the refrigerator needed to keep it cold are both proportional to stored energy.
